title: Woodpecker-Inspired Bike Helmet Tops Safety Rankings
summary:
A small Vancouver company called Pikio Labs has taken the top spot in Virginia Tech’s bike-helmet safety ratings with a design inspired by woodpeckers.

Helmet tests once focused mainly on straight-on hits. Researchers also care about twisting forces during a crash, which can raise concussion risk. Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings measure both kinds of impact and score lower as better. The Pikio Si Oblik helmet scored 4.61, well ahead of the previous best Canyon Deflectr at 6.82.

Founder Daniel Abram spent years studying impact protection, including work at Simon Fraser University and earlier companies. The Oblik system divides the usual foam liner into sections that can flex, move, or detach on hard hits, helping manage both direct and twisting forces. Dual-density foam absorbs straight impacts.

Other designs take different approaches. MIPS uses a low-friction layer that can shift slightly at the start of an impact. Some rivals use floating outer panels. Abram says a typical helmet may have about eight to 10 parts, while the Pikio Si uses around 80, which helps explain its $379 price.

In a WIRED road test, the medium-size helmet weighed 279 grams, felt comfortable, and had 17 vents. If a helmet is seriously crashed, it must be replaced; Pikio has offered a discount when damaged helmets are returned for study. Abram said four returned helmets had already helped the company learn and had protected riders.

Whether Oblik becomes a widely licensed technology remains to be seen, but for now it gives other makers a new safety score to chase.
why_it_matters: Better helmet design can reduce injury risk for kids and adults who bike. Independent test scores help families compare safety claims with measured results.
